newsitem.title: zaire: Zaire army chief seeks to control arms supplies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army chief seeks to control arms supplies.

text.p: Zaire's armed forces chief of staff told the government on Wednesday to let the army take charge of weapons purchases and distribution, suggesting a deepening rift over the conduct of the country's civil war.

At the same time, General Mahele Lieko Bokoungo played down rumours of an army coup saying that the state was not dead and there was no provision in the constitution for the army taking power in the event of an institutional void.

His comments, in a statement and at a news conference in the capital Kinshasa, coincided with an opposition campaign to oust Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who was in Kenya for regional talks on Zaire's war.
Mahele said Kengo's fate was a political problem.
"The army is apolitical. We are observers and we are observing. The state is not dead," he added.
Asked whether the army would take over in the event of an institutional void, he replied:
"If it is provided for in the constitution, yes, but I think that in the constitution there is nothing to that effect."
Zaire's interim parliament voted on Tuesday to sack Kengo.

Supporters of the prime minister and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, who was in hospital in Europe, say the vote was not legally binding as it fell short of a three quarters majority required by the transitional constitution.

But state radio added weight to the opposition campaign by reporting that parliament had in fact sacked the government. "Zaire no longer has a government. The governmenet has been dismissed by the High Council of the Republic-Transitional Parliament," it said.
Mahele, appointed by Mobutu in December, denounced looting by his notoriously ill-disciplined soldiers and gave Kinshasa residents numbers to telephone over problems in the capital.
Army looting at regular intervals during Mobutu's three decades in power has alientated local Zaireans and now works in favour of rebels advancing in the east and south.
But in his statement, read by a fellow officer, Mahele said the government should take care of soldiers basic needs.

"You, those in power, take care of the fate of our soldiers," the statement said. "He demanded that the acquisition and management of logistics of the armed forces should henceforth be the responsibility of the army," it added.
Mahele's remarks were the first since a January 20 army counter-offensive flopped as rebels advanced on several fronts.
Earlier, a spokesman for the main opposition of veteran radical Etienne Tshisekedi said he would begin contacts soon on forming a government to negotiate with the rebels.
But heavy rain swept Kinshasa where opposition militants showed no sign of staging threatened anti-Kengo protests.

A spokesman for Mobutu, who has been having follow-up treatment for prostate cancer in Monaco, said he would leave hospital on Thursday. Airport officials in the French town of Nice said Mobutu's private plane was standing by to take him home. No date has been set for his departure.

Under the interim constitution, the head of the transitional parliament should succeed Mobutu in the event of his death. Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo resigned from the job in 1995 and has not been replaced.
A Mobutu supporter is one of the deputy speakers, an opposition supporter the other.
